sections.title: Masses and Springs · Theory and Prediction
One mass, two directions

teaching.text: A mass on a spring **oscillates**, which means it moves back and forth around **equilibrium**, its resting position. Displacing the mass stretches or squeezes the spring, and the spring answers with a force aimed back at equilibrium.
children: Because of its **inertia**, the moving mass carries on past equilibrium and displaces the spring on the far side.
The spring then pushes or pulls the other way, sends the mass back and starts the next cycle.

teaching.text: The mass can travel in two directions.
children: **Longitudinal motion** runs along the spring, so the spring lengthens and shortens.
**Transverse motion** runs across the spring. The two segments are already under tension, and lifting or lowering the mass angles their pull back toward the resting line.

teaching.text: Each side of the cycle has its own restoring direction.
children: On one side of equilibrium, the spring acts toward the center from that side.
After the mass crosses, the displacement reverses and the force reverses with it. Inertia carries the mass across, and the restoring force brings it back, over and over.

teaching.text: The two directions repeat at the same **frequency**, **0.5 Hz**, or one cycle every two seconds.
children: They match because both have the same mass and the same total restoring stiffness.
The model has no damping, so each cycle is as large as the one before.

sections.title: Mass and stiffness change the rate

teaching.text: An oscillator’s rate depends on its **mass** and its **stiffness**. Three systems run together, and each comparison changes one property while holding the other fixed.
children: The reference has mass **m** and stiffness **K** and runs at **0.5 Hz**.
Quadrupling the mass to **4m** slows it to **0.25 Hz**.
Quadrupling the stiffness to **4K** speeds it to **1 Hz**.

teaching.text: **More mass means a lower frequency.**
children: A heavier mass takes more force to speed up, slow down and reverse.
With the same spring, each cycle takes longer, and four times the mass gives half the rate.

teaching.text: **More stiffness means a higher frequency.**
children: A stiffer spring pulls back harder for the same displacement.
The mass reverses sooner and completes more cycles per second, and four times the stiffness gives twice the rate.
Mass is the system’s resistance to changes in motion, and stiffness is the strength of its return.

teaching.text: The rate is found by counting complete cycles over equal stretches of time.
children: **Amplitude**, the distance the mass travels, is a separate property.

Each longitudinal and transverse pair matches because both share the same **effective restoring stiffness**, meaning the restoring action in the direction of motion. For transverse motion, that stiffness comes from the tension and layout of the spring segments.

sections.title: Two masses have two normal modes

teaching.text: Two equal masses linked by three equal springs between fixed ends have **two normal modes**. In a **normal mode**, every part of the system moves at one frequency and keeps a fixed relationship to the other parts.
In **Mode 1**, the two masses move in step, in the same direction.
children: Their spacing stays nearly constant, so the middle spring barely changes length.
This mode runs at **0.4 Hz**.

teaching.text: In **Mode 2**, the masses move in opposite directions.
children: The middle spring is squeezed and stretched hard on every cycle.
The added restoring force makes this the faster mode, at about **1.73 times** the frequency of Mode 1.

teaching.text: Each mode is a pattern of the whole chain.
children: Both masses move in both modes.
The masses and springs are identical in the two patterns, and the difference lies in how the masses move relative to each other.

teaching.text: Both modes can run together on the same masses.
children: At each mass the two motions add, strengthening where they agree and canceling where they disagree. This is **superposition**.
The combined motion in the bottom row is the exact sum of the two modes and carries both frequencies. The longitudinal and transverse chains follow the same pattern.

sections.title: Pop quiz
Three masses have three normal modes

teaching.text: Three equal masses with four equal springs between fixed ends have **three normal modes**.
**Mode 1** moves all three masses in the same direction.
children: The middle mass swings the farthest, and the outer two swing less.
This is the lowest mode, at **0.32 Hz**.

teaching.text: **Mode 2** moves the two outer masses in opposite directions.
children: The pulls on the middle mass cancel, so it stays at equilibrium.
A point that stays still throughout a mode is a **node**.
This mode runs at about **1.85 times** the lowest frequency.

teaching.text: **Mode 3** moves the outer masses together and the middle mass against them.
children: Each mass now moves opposite to its neighbor, so every spring stretches and squeezes strongly.
This is the highest mode, at about **2.41 times** the lowest frequency.

teaching.text: The more neighbors oppose each other, the faster the mode.
children: Opposing neighbors stretch the springs more, which strengthens the restoring force and speeds up the cycle.
All three masses take part in every mode. The colors follow each mass, and the resting marks give the position each displacement starts from.

teaching.text: The frequency ratios are specific to this chain.
children: When the modes combine, their motions add at each mass.
The middle mass moves in the mixture because Modes 1 and 3 move it, even though Mode 2 holds it still.

sections.title: One more mass, one more mode

teaching.text: Every movable mass adds one **normal mode** in the modeled direction. The atlas sets chains of one through six masses in rows, with mode numbers in columns, for **21** patterns in all.
children: Each chain has equal masses, one more spring than masses and two fixed ends.
A chain of three masses fills three columns, and a chain of six fills six.

teaching.text: In every chain, **Mode 1** is the broadest pattern, with all masses moving together.
children: Each higher mode adds one more group moving the opposite way.
More reversals put more neighbors in opposition, which stretches the springs more, strengthens the restoring force and raises the frequency.

teaching.text: The fixed ends stay still in every mode.
children: A mass that stays still within one mode is a node of that pattern while the others keep moving.
Higher modes use the very same masses and springs in a different arrangement, and the mode number names the arrangement.

teaching.text: Colors mark the mode number, and rows mark the number of masses.
children: Every pattern is drawn with the same largest displacement, so frequency is read from the repetition rate.
**Amplitude** is how far the parts move, and frequency is how often they repeat.
Chains of separate masses have frequency spacings that differ from the whole-number spacing of an ideal continuous string.

sections.title: A fixed–fixed string combines harmonics

teaching.text: A **fixed–fixed string** is clamped at both ends, which makes both ends **nodes**.
children: **Mode 1** fits one half-wave between the ends.
Modes 2, 3, 4 and 5 fit two, three, four and five half-waves.

teaching.text: Packing more half-waves into the same length shortens the wavelength and raises the frequency.
children: The five modes run at **100, 200, 300, 400 and 500 Hz**.
These are consecutive **harmonics**, whole-number multiples of the **fundamental**, and they include both odd and even multiples.

teaching.text: All five modes can share the string at once.
children: Their motions add at every point, so the overall outline keeps changing while each component stays regular.
A point can go nearly still through cancellation and then move strongly as the modes drift back into step. Every component is present the whole time.

teaching.text: The display is slowed **250** times, so 100 Hz appears at **0.4 Hz**.
children: Slowing every mode by the same factor keeps their relative rates intact.

teaching.text: A **pickup** placed **17%** of the way along the string records the motion at that one point.
children: Its **spectrum** has one peak for each component, with frequency along one axis and amplitude along the other.
The mode strengths were set so the five peaks come out equal at this point. A pickup elsewhere would record different heights.

sections.title: A membrane combines spatial modes

teaching.text: A **membrane** is a vibrating surface with fixed edges, and its modes carry two-number labels. The two numbers count the moving regions along the two directions of the surface.
children: **(1,1)** is a single region moving as one.
**(2,1)** and **(1,2)** split the surface in two, one along each direction.
**(2,2)** makes four regions, and **(3,1)** makes three along one direction.
Neighboring regions move opposite to each other, separated by **node** lines that stay still.

teaching.text: The five modes add at every point into one changing surface.
children: Where they agree they reinforce, and where they disagree they cancel.
The combined panel uses a smaller vertical scale than the single-mode panels.

teaching.text: A node is still for the whole cycle.
children: A moving region passes through the resting level for an instant each cycle and then keeps moving.
Following one region as it rises, crosses and falls, while its neighbor moves the other way, separates moving regions from nodes.
The two numbers describe how the surface divides into regions.

teaching.text: A **pickup** at one marked point records its motion, and the **spectrum** there has one peak per mode.
children: The strengths were chosen to make the five peaks equal at that point.

The frequencies **100, 200, 300, 400 and 500 Hz** were **assigned for the illustration** instead of calculated from this rectangle’s own resonances. They model how evenly spaced frequencies combine on a surface.

sections.title: Theory makes a measurable prediction

teaching.text: The **scientific method** rests on stating very clear theories about the world, usually as **differential equations**.
children: A differential equation describes how the quantities in a system change.
Solving it yields a **prediction** of what a real measurement should find.

teaching.text: The theory here treats the **vocal folds as a membrane**.
children: A vibrating membrane produces a wave whose spectrum has **equidistant peaks**, called **harmonics**.
The equations are of the same kind as those for springs and membranes, with somewhat more detail.

teaching.text: The prediction follows directly.
children: Any person’s **laryngeal vibration** signal should have a spectrum with **equidistant harmonics**, peaks separated by equal intervals.
Testing it means recording real vocal-fold vibration and examining the spacing of the peaks. Even spacing supports the theory, and uneven spacing challenges it.

teaching.text: The spectrum is the part of the signal that carries the prediction.
children: Vibration alone is expected either way, so the evenly spaced peaks are what the experiment checks.
The membrane animation uses assigned harmonic frequencies, so it pictures the idea, while a recording of real vocal folds tests it. The experiment is proposed here, ready to be carried out.

sections.title: One fixed end and one free end

teaching.text: A **fixed–free system** is held at one end and free at the other.
children: The fixed end must be a **node**, with no movement.
The free end must be an **antinode**, the place of largest movement.

teaching.text: Shapes that meet both conditions fit odd numbers of **quarter-waves**.
children: The first mode fits one quarter-wave.
The next fit three, five and seven quarter-waves.
These are the **first, third, fifth and seventh harmonics**, so the second allowed mode is the third harmonic.

teaching.text: Odd counts are the only ones that leave the fixed end still and the free end moving.
children: An even count would put a node at the free end.
Higher modes fit shorter waves into the same length, so they repeat faster.

teaching.text: The four modes run at **100, 300, 500 and 700 Hz**, slowed **250** times for display.
children: Given equal strengths, they produce four equal peaks in the spectrum measured at the free end.
An antinode swings through the resting line to the opposite side on every cycle, while the fixed end stays still.

teaching.text: The fixed–fixed and fixed–free strings were **tuned separately** to share a fundamental.
children: With the same length and wave speed, freeing one end would cut the fundamental in half.
The matching labels therefore come from separate tuning, and the effect of the free end is to halve the fundamental.

sections.title: Masses and Springs in Speech Production
Dynamic systems in economic stabilization

teaching.text: A **dynamic system** changes over time as its parts act on one another, and that idea reaches well beyond springs. Economics has its own dynamic systems.
children: **Woodford’s theory**, **Dynamic Stochastic General Equilibrium** or **DSGE**, models an economy as a dynamic system.
Its name combines change over time, random shocks and many linked markets that settle toward balance together.

teaching.text: The stabilization picture follows two quantities through time.
children: The **black curve** is **unemployment**.
The **gray curve** is **inflation**.
Before stabilization, both swing through large, jagged peaks and dips, and afterward the swings are smaller and smoother.

teaching.text: **Stabilization** means making those swings smaller.
children: The economy keeps changing, and unemployment and inflation stay two separate quantities.
The goal is to keep away from harmful extremes such as very high unemployment or runaway inflation.

teaching.text: Physical oscillators and economies share one central question, what drives a fluctuation and what calms it.
children: In a spring, inertia and the restoring force drive the swing.
In an economy, shocks and the responses of its parts drive it. The calmer curves picture the goal of stabilization.

sections.title: Mass, stiffness, position, and frequency

teaching.text: The **principles of mass–spring systems** sum up how these systems behave in seven statements.
**Mass and stiffness pull frequency in opposite directions.**
children: More mass lowers the frequency, since a heavier load turns around more slowly.
More stiffness raises the frequency, since a stronger restoring force reverses the motion sooner.

teaching.text: **An n-mass system has n modes**, each with a higher frequency than the last.
**Position decides how much a change matters.**
children: Added mass lowers a mode’s frequency in proportion to how much that mass moves in the mode.
Added stiffness raises a mode’s frequency in proportion to how much that spring stretches or compresses.
Maximal movement comes with no stretching, and maximal stretching comes with no movement. Neighbors that move together keep their spacing, so motion and compression peak in different places.

teaching.text: One change can therefore matter in one mode and barely register in another.
children: It matters where the mode moves or stretches strongly.
It matters little at a node of that mode, and that same node can move in other modes or in a mixture.

teaching.text: **Endpoints set the harmonic pattern.**
children: A **fixed–fixed system** has harmonics at whole-number multiples of the base frequency, because the base shape fits a whole number of times into each higher mode.
A **fixed–free system** has harmonics at **odd multiples** of the base frequency, because the base shape fits an odd number of times into each higher mode.

sections.title: A local change affects two modes differently

teaching.text: The **pop quiz** asks what happens to two modes when mass or stiffness is added at one spot on a string, just left of the midpoint.
The two modes use that spot in opposite ways.
children: **Mode 4** moves the spot strongly, while its neighbors move along with it, so little stretching happens there.
**Mode 5** moves the spot very little, while its neighbors move differently, so the string stretches and compresses strongly there.

teaching.text: **Adding mass** acts on movement.
children: Mode 4 carries the extra mass through a large swing, so its frequency falls.
Mode 5 barely moves the spot, so its frequency stays about the same.
Mass lowers frequency in the modes that move it.

teaching.text: **Adding stiffness** acts on stretching.
children: Mode 5 stretches the spot strongly, so the stiffer spring adds restoring force and raises its frequency.
Mode 4 barely stretches the spot, so its frequency stays about the same.

teaching.text: Adding **both** at that spot **lowers Mode 4 and raises Mode 5**.
children: The spot is the same in both modes.
Its role differs, mainly movement in Mode 4 and mainly stretching in Mode 5, measured over a whole cycle of each mode.

sections.title: Air in a fixed–free tube has modes

teaching.text: The air in the vocal tract behaves like a chain of masses and springs.
children: Moving air has **inertia** and keeps moving.
Squeezed air pushes back, and the spring-like links in the model represent that restoring effect.
The air elements move **longitudinally**, back and forth along the tube, oscillating around their usual places.

teaching.text: The tube is a **fixed–free** system.
children: The **glottis** is the fixed end.
The open **lips** are the free end.

teaching.text: The lowest two patterns match the lowest two formants.
children: **Mode 1 is F1-like**, the tube’s lowest resonance.
**Mode 2 is F2-like**, with one more reversal along the tube.
In the uniform tube, Mode 2 runs **three times** as fast as Mode 1, the odd-multiple pattern of a fixed–free system. Changing the tract’s shape changes that ratio.

teaching.text: Each mode is a coordinated pattern of the whole column of air.
children: In some places, neighboring elements travel together and keep their spacing.
In others, their gaps close and open over and over.

teaching.text: Three markers place the vowel constrictions.
children: **/a/** is about **one-third** of the way from the glottis.
**/i/** is about **two-thirds** of the way.
**/u/** is at the **lips**.

Each marker is the same physical spot in both modes. Added mass acts where a mode moves strongly, and added springiness acts where it compresses strongly, so one narrowing can push F1 and F2 differently.

The two high vowels narrow the tract at different places.
children: **Dean** is **high and front**, with its constriction about **two-thirds** of the way from the glottis to the lips.
**Dune** is **high and back**, with its constriction at the **lips**.
They share a height and differ in where they narrow.

teaching.text: The two low vowels sit at the bottom.
children: **Dan** is **low and front**.
**Don** is **low and back**, with its constriction about **one-third** of the way from the glottis.

teaching.text: **Done** is **central** and marked **“No constriction.”**
children: It is the open reference shape.

teaching.text: Each label captures its own feature.
children: High and low describe tongue height.

children: **Movement** is how far an air element travels.
**Compression** is how the gap between neighbors changes. Narrower gaps are compression, and wider gaps are **rarefaction**, or thinned-out air.
Neighbors can travel together with steady spacing, or squeeze and spread around an element that hardly moves.

teaching.text: The animation splits one air column into its patterns.
children: The moving **Schwa** row is the uniform reference.
The **F1, F2 and F3** rows are the first three resonances of that column.
The closed left end holds the air still, and the open right end lets it move. Higher modes pack more alternating regions of movement and compression into the tube.

teaching.text: Compression and movement play the roles of spring and mass.
children: Crowded air pushes back toward normal spacing, which supplies the restoring force.
Moving air keeps going because of inertia.
Together they keep the air oscillating around its usual positions.

teaching.text: Strong movement and strong compression occupy different places.
children: Where movement is large, the region carries a lot of moving mass.
Where spacing changes a lot, the region supplies strong restoring force while its central element stays nearly put.

teaching.text: Tracking one element over a cycle measures its movement, and tracking its gaps measures compression.
children: Added mass acts where movement is strong.
Added stiffness acts where compression is strong.
Those places shift from mode to mode, and each row is its own resonance of the same air.

sections.title: The source supplies harmonics and the filter shapes their heights

teaching.text: **Source–filter theory** splits speech into a **source**, the vibration of the vocal folds, and a **filter**, the vocal tract that shapes that vibration.
The glottal source produces a **harmonic comb**.
children: It repeats at a **fundamental frequency**, **F0**, with harmonics at whole-number multiples of F0.
In the example, the harmonics sit **100 Hz** apart and run up to **4000 Hz**.
Before the tract acts, they are evenly spaced vertical lines of equal height.

teaching.text: The tract filter **sculpts the heights** of the harmonics.
children: Harmonics near the tract’s resonances, the **formants**, grow stronger, and the rest grow weaker.
Every line keeps its position, and only its height changes.
The outline of those heights is the **spectral envelope**, and that envelope is the vowel.

teaching.text: In the schwa example, four resonance regions, **F1 through F4**, shape the comb, with the strongest group at low frequency.
The horizontal axis gives frequency, and the vertical axis gives amplitude.
children: A taller line is a stronger component.
**F0** is the source’s repetition rate, and **F1** is the tract’s lowest resonance.
The vowel is made of many harmonics, with the formants deciding which of them are strong.

sections.title: The /i/ filter keeps F1 low and F2 high

teaching.text: The **/i/ filter** combines a **low F1** with a **high F2**, and it acts on the same 100 Hz comb.
children: One strong group of harmonics sits near the low end.
The next strong group sits far higher, past a weak stretch.
More strong groups follow around **F3** and **F4**, near **3000** and **3600 Hz**.

teaching.text: The source lines keep their even spacing and positions.
children: The tract changes only their heights.
The filter’s effect therefore stands apart from the source’s repetition.

teaching.text: This low-F1, high-F2 pattern comes from the front constriction of /i/.
children: The narrowing adds mass where Mode 1 moves and stiffness where Mode 2 compresses.
F1 drops and F2 climbs, which pushes the two formants far apart.

teaching.text: Each line is read in two ways.
children: Its horizontal position is its **frequency**.
Its height is its **amplitude**.
A tall line near the low end is a strong low-frequency component.

teaching.text: The harmonic lines sample the broad formant regions.
children: The envelope traced by their heights is the vowel /i/ in this schematic.

sections.title: The /a/ filter raises F1 and lowers F2

teaching.text: The **/a/ filter** has a **higher F1** and a **lower F2** than /i/. Here **F1 is at 750 Hz** and **F2 near 1200 Hz**, so the first two formants sit close together.
children: **F3** and **F4** stay higher, near **2600** and **3500 Hz**.
The source is unchanged, and the new tract shape makes a new vowel.

teaching.text: The filter reshapes the harmonic **strengths**.
children: Moving a formant shifts the favored region along the frequency axis.
Changing a harmonic’s amplitude changes its height.
The spectrum records these as two separate kinds of change.

teaching.text: A formant can sit **between two source harmonics**.
children: The 750 Hz F1 target falls between the **700** and **800 Hz** harmonics.
Those two nearby harmonics become strong, and the source supplies no line exactly at 750 Hz.

teaching.text: A **formant** is a resonance region of the filter.
children: A **harmonic** is a frequency component of the source.
The filter decides how strong each harmonic is, and the harmonics reveal where the formants are.

sections.title: A spectrogram places successive spectra in time

teaching.text: A **spectrum** shows **one instant**, and a **spectrogram** **stacks many spectra over time**.
A spectrum describes the frequency components of one short slice of sound.
children: Frequency runs across, and amplitude runs up.
The example uses three successive spectra of **/i/** and three of **/a/**.

teaching.text: A spectrogram arranges those slices from left to right in time.
children: Its frequency axis runs upward, so a peak at the right side of a spectrum becomes a mark high in the spectrogram.
Moving right in a spectrogram means moving later in time.

teaching.text: **Height in the spectrum becomes darkness in the spectrogram.**
children: In grayscale, **black is high amplitude, gray is medium and white is low**.
Vertical position gives frequency, and darkness gives strength.
A darkening band is growing stronger, and a rising band is moving to higher frequency.

teaching.text: From **/i/** to **/a/**, **F1 rises and F2 falls**.
children: The two lowest bands draw toward each other.
The higher bands stay above them with smaller shifts.
The spectrogram tracks the tract’s resonances as they change over time.

sections.title: Reflection prompt
Wide harmonic spacing makes formants harder to identify

teaching.text: Formants are easiest to identify when the source harmonics are **close together**. Each harmonic samples the tract’s response, and many closely spaced samples trace each formant clearly.
With harmonics at **100, 200, 300, 400 Hz** and onward, a vowel with **F1 at 300** and **F2 at 2100 Hz** shapes the amplitudes of many harmonics.
children: Several lines cluster around each formant.
Their heights rise and fall with the filter, so each formant region stands out.

teaching.text: A higher **F0** spaces the harmonics farther apart.
children: With harmonics at **250, 500, 750** and onward, fewer lines fall near each formant.
A formant can sit between two harmonics, and one strong line can sit near a formant without marking its center.
Telling harmonics from formants becomes very hard.

teaching.text: Higher voices space the harmonics wider still.
children: A **toddler’s** harmonics could be **400, 800** and onward.
A **soprano’s** could be **800, 1600, 2400** and onward.
Across the three spectra and spectrograms, closely spaced components give way to a few isolated traces.

teaching.text: The filter itself is unchanged.
children: The tract keeps the same resonances.
The source now offers fewer frequencies to reveal that same filter.

sections.title: Homework 4 lab reminder
Speech → Neural Networks
Five membrane modes combine into one motion

teaching.text: A **membrane** is a vibrating surface with fixed edges, and its modes carry two-number labels. The two numbers count the moving regions along the two directions of the surface.
children: **(1,1)** is a single region moving as one.
**(2,1)** and **(1,2)** split the surface in two, one along each direction.
**(2,2)** makes four regions, and **(3,1)** makes three along one direction.
Neighboring regions move opposite to each other, separated by **node** lines that stay still.

teaching.text: The five modes add at every point into one changing surface.
children: Where they agree they reinforce, and where they disagree they cancel.
The combined panel uses a smaller vertical scale than the single-mode panels.

teaching.text: A node is still for the whole cycle.
children: A moving region passes through the resting level for an instant each cycle and then keeps moving.
Following one region as it rises, crosses and falls, while its neighbor moves the other way, separates moving regions from nodes.
The two numbers describe how the surface divides into regions.

teaching.text: A **pickup** at one marked point records its motion, and the **spectrum** there has one peak per mode.
children: The strengths were chosen to make the five peaks equal at that point.

The frequencies **100, 200, 300, 400 and 500 Hz** were **assigned for the illustration** instead of calculated from this rectangle’s own resonances. They model how evenly spaced frequencies combine on a surface.

sections.title: A fixed end and a free end select odd harmonics

teaching.text: A **fixed–free system** is held at one end and free at the other.
children: The fixed end must be a **node**, with no movement.
The free end must be an **antinode**, the place of largest movement.

teaching.text: Shapes that meet both conditions fit odd numbers of **quarter-waves**.
children: The first mode fits one quarter-wave.
The next fit three, five and seven quarter-waves.
These are the **first, third, fifth and seventh harmonics**, so the second allowed mode is the third harmonic.

teaching.text: Odd counts are the only ones that leave the fixed end still and the free end moving.
children: An even count would put a node at the free end.
Higher modes fit shorter waves into the same length, so they repeat faster.

teaching.text: The four modes run at **100, 300, 500 and 700 Hz**, slowed **250** times for display.
children: Given equal strengths, they produce four equal peaks in the spectrum measured at the free end.
An antinode swings through the resting line to the opposite side on every cycle, while the fixed end stays still.

teaching.text: The fixed–fixed and fixed–free strings were **tuned separately** to share a fundamental.
children: With the same length and wave speed, freeing one end would cut the fundamental in half.
The matching labels therefore come from separate tuning, and the effect of the free end is to halve the fundamental.

sections.title: Quarter-wavelength packets explain the allowed modes

teaching.text: A **quarter-wavelength** links a **node** to an **antinode**. The fixed–free string needs a node at its fixed bottom and an antinode at its free top.
children: **One quarter-wave** fits exactly between those two ends.
That is the simplest allowed pattern, with no still point inside.

teaching.text: Quarter-waves are added **two at a time**.
children: One more alone would end at a node, which the free top cannot have.
Two more end at an antinode again.
The allowed patterns hold **one, three, five and seven quarter-waves** in the same length.

teaching.text: More sections give shorter wavelengths.
children: At the same wave speed, shorter waves repeat faster, so each pattern climbs in frequency.

teaching.text: The demonstration adds one packet at a time to every mode that contains it.
children: The four modes hold **1, 3, 5 and 7** packets, which match the odd harmonics.
The numbered pieces label regions of the standing shape and stay where they are.
The string swings back and forth while the pattern’s still points hold their positions.

teaching.text: The endpoint conditions alone produce the odd harmonics.
children: Every allowed count ends on an antinode at the free top.
Only odd counts do that, so only odd multiples of the fundamental appear.

sections.title: Air moves longitudinally in vocal-tract modes

teaching.text: The air in the vocal tract behaves like a chain of masses and springs.
children: Moving air has **inertia** and keeps moving.
Squeezed air pushes back, and the spring-like links in the model represent that restoring effect.
The air elements move **longitudinally**, back and forth along the tube, oscillating around their usual places.

teaching.text: The tube is a **fixed–free** system.
children: The **glottis** is the fixed end.
The open **lips** are the free end.

teaching.text: The lowest two patterns match the lowest two formants.
children: **Mode 1 is F1-like**, the tube’s lowest resonance.
**Mode 2 is F2-like**, with one more reversal along the tube.
In the uniform tube, Mode 2 runs **three times** as fast as Mode 1, the odd-multiple pattern of a fixed–free system. Changing the tract’s shape changes that ratio.

teaching.text: Each mode is a coordinated pattern of the whole column of air.
children: In some places, neighboring elements travel together and keep their spacing.
In others, their gaps close and open over and over.

teaching.text: Three markers place the vowel constrictions.
children: **/a/** is about **one-third** of the way from the glottis.
**/i/** is about **two-thirds** of the way.
**/u/** is at the **lips**.

Each marker is the same physical spot in both modes. Added mass acts where a mode moves strongly, and added springiness acts where it compresses strongly, so one narrowing can push F1 and F2 differently.

sections.title: Track air motion separately from compression

teaching.text: Every point in an air column has a **movement** and a **compression**.
children: **Movement** is the distance an air element travels.
**Compression** is the change in spacing between neighbors.
Neighbors can travel together with steady gaps, and gaps can close and open strongly around a nearly still point.

teaching.text: Each property has its own reading.
children: One circle followed through a cycle gives movement.
The gaps between neighboring circles give compression, squeezed in some regions and spread in others.

teaching.text: Together they act as spring and mass.
children: Changing compression provides a **spring-like restoring effect**, as crowded air pushes back toward normal spacing.
**Inertia** keeps the air moving as that push changes.

teaching.text: The tube’s ends set the layout.
children: The **closed end** holds movement back.
The **open end** lets the air move.
Each higher mode places its alternating regions at its own positions in the tube.

teaching.text: The moving **Schwa** reference and the **F1, F2 and F3** rows are resonances of one air system.
children: A constriction can act on moving mass in one mode and on compression in another.
Its effect depends on the mode and on where it sits.

sections.title: Compare positions within an air mode

teaching.text: The **pop quiz** labels six spots along the air column, **A** to **F**, and asks how each one behaves.
children: Each spot is followed through a full cycle.
Its air element’s travel gives its movement.
The spacing changes around it give its compression.
A full cycle is what reveals the spot’s usual behavior.

teaching.text: At a spot with strong **movement**, added mass is what counts.
children: More **effective mass** is slower to speed up and reverse.
The cycle lengthens, and the resonance **falls**.

teaching.text: At a spot with strong **compression change**, added stiffness is what counts.
children: More **stiffness** pushes the air back toward its spacing more strongly.
The cycle shortens, and the resonance **rises**.

teaching.text: **Modes 1, 2 and 3** lay these regions out differently.
children: A spot that moves strongly in one mode can be squeezed strongly in another.
A prediction needs both the position and the mode.

sections.title: Vowel positions change where the tract is narrowed

teaching.text: Vowels are classified by **tongue height** and **front–back position**, and each one narrows the airway at a particular place. Five words sit on a chart of those two dimensions.
The two high vowels narrow the tract at different places.
children: **Dean** is **high and front**, with its constriction about **two-thirds** of the way from the glottis to the lips.
**Dune** is **high and back**, with its constriction at the **lips**.
They share a height and differ in where they narrow.

teaching.text: The two low vowels sit at the bottom.
children: **Dan** is **low and front**.
**Don** is **low and back**, with its constriction about **one-third** of the way from the glottis.

teaching.text: **Done** is **central** and marked **“No constriction.”**
children: It is the open reference shape.

teaching.text: Each label captures its own feature.
children: High and low describe tongue height.
Front and back describe where the tongue sits along the mouth.
The fraction gives distance along the air path from the glottis.

teaching.text: The constriction’s location ties the articulation to the sound.
children: Narrowing the airway changes the local mass-like and spring-like behavior of the air.
How each formant responds depends on how its mode moves and compresses that spot.

sections.title: A constriction changes inertia and restoring stiffness

teaching.text: A **constriction** narrows the airway and raises two properties of the air at once.
It raises **stiffness**.
children: Compressed air resists further compression more strongly.
At a place where the air is **heavily compressed**, a constriction **raises the frequency**.

teaching.text: It raises **mass**.
children: Bunching air up increases its density.
At a place where the air **moves a lot**, a constriction adds moving mass and **lowers the frequency**.

teaching.text: Both increases happen together, and each one acts in a different region.
children: The parts of a vibrating medium that **move the most** alternate with the parts that **compress and expand the most**.
Each mode places those regions at its own positions.

teaching.text: The way to tell the effects apart is to follow the air through a cycle.
children: One element’s travel measures how much mass is being carried there.
The opening and closing of the gaps beside it measures compression, the source of the restoring force.
Watching both through a cycle reveals which effect governs that spot in that mode.

teaching.text: One narrowing can therefore act mainly through **mass** for one formant and mainly through **stiffness** for another.
children: One formant falls and the other rises.
Both rules hold exactly as before, mass lowering frequency where air moves and stiffness raising it where air compresses.

sections.title: Use both modes to interpret the same tract location

teaching.text: **Mode 1** and **Mode 2** are two resonances of one air column, held at the glottis and open at the lips.
children: Both move the air strongly near the lips.
Mode 2 adds one more reversal inside the tube and arranges movement and compression its own way.

teaching.text: Markers at the **back**, the **front** and the **lips** sit at the same places in both modes.
children: A narrowing at any marker changes that region for both modes together.

teaching.text: What the narrowing does depends on each mode’s activity at the marker.
children: Strong **movement** brings in the mass-like effect, which slows the vibration.
Strong **compression** brings in the spring-like effect, which speeds it up.
A single narrowing can therefore push **F1** and **F2** in different directions.

teaching.text: The two modes follow a set ratio in the ideal tube.
children: In the uniform reference, Mode 2 runs at **three times** the frequency of Mode 1.
A changed tract shape changes the formants and that ratio.

teaching.text: **Formants** are tract resonances that change with tract shape.
children: **Harmonics** are source components whose spacing comes from vocal-fold repetition.

sections.title: Lip loading lowers both F1 and F2 in the /u/ model

teaching.text: The **/u/ model** loads the open lips, the **free end** of the air column. Larger elements at the lips represent more **effective mass**, meaning more air that must be moved back and forth there.
Both lowest modes move strongly at the free end.
children: In **Mode 1**, **motion dominates** at the lips.
In **Mode 2**, **motion dominates** at the lips as well.

teaching.text: A larger moving load takes longer to speed up and reverse.
children: Wherever motion dominates, the added load lengthens each cycle.
Both modes slow, giving **F1 down and F2 down** relative to the uniform tube.

teaching.text: The two rows compare one lip location across two resonance patterns.
children: Each pattern is arranged differently inside the tube, yet both move strongly at the lips.
The extra load slows both while F1 remains the lower formant and F2 the higher one.
Each change is measured against that mode’s own uniform reference.

teaching.text: The common direction comes from the lip region’s role in both modes.
children: Here motion dominates in both, so loading lowers both.
The air keeps oscillating around its usual positions, with the larger elements marking the added load.

sections.title: A front constriction separates the effects on F1 and F2

teaching.text: The **/i/ constriction** is near the front, about **two-thirds** of the way from the glottis to the lips. One physical region is narrowed, and that region does a different job in each mode.
In **Mode 1**, **mass motion dominates** at the narrowing.
children: The air there moves strongly.
Narrowing adds effective moving mass, which slows the reversal.
**F1 goes down**.

teaching.text: In **Mode 2**, **springiness dominates** at the narrowing.
children: The air there is strongly squeezed and stretched.
Narrowing strengthens the restoring response, which speeds the reversal.
**F2 goes up**.

teaching.text: The region stays in one place, and its role changes from mode to mode.
children: Where neighbors travel together, moving load is what counts.
Where neighbors keep pressing together and pulling apart, the restoring response is what counts.

teaching.text: The outcome is **lower F1 and higher F2** than the uniform tube.
children: The mass effect governs F1, and the spring effect governs F2.
One constriction therefore moves the two formants in opposite directions, by two separate causes.

sections.title: A back constriction reverses the F1 and F2 pattern

teaching.text: The **/a/ constriction** is farther back, about **one-third** of the way from the glottis to the lips. At this spot the two modes trade roles compared with /i/.
In **Mode 1**, **springiness dominates** at the narrowing.
children: The air there is strongly compressed.
Narrowing adds restoring force, so the cycle speeds up and **F1 goes up**.

teaching.text: In **Mode 2**, **mass motion dominates** at the narrowing.
children: The air there moves strongly.
Narrowing adds effective moving mass, so the cycle slows and **F2 goes down**.

teaching.text: Both rows narrow the same back location, and each row is its own coordinated motion.
children: In one pattern, the spot moves little while its neighbors squeeze and spread around it.
In the other, the spot moves a lot while its spacing barely changes.
That is why springiness governs Mode 1 and moving mass governs Mode 2 here.

teaching.text: The outcome is **higher F1 and lower F2**, the mirror image of /i/.
children: Moving the constriction changes which role matters most, while mass and stiffness keep their usual effects.
The arrows give the predicted direction of each change.

sections.title: Air motion and compression in the vocal-tract modes

teaching.text: Each spot in an air column can be described by its **movement** and its **compression**.
children: **Movement** is how far an air element travels.
**Compression** is how the gap between neighbors changes. Narrower gaps are compression, and wider gaps are **rarefaction**, or thinned-out air.
Neighbors can travel together with steady spacing, or squeeze and spread around an element that hardly moves.

The **F1, F2 and F3** rows are the first three resonances of that column.
The closed left end holds the air still, and the open right end lets it move. Higher modes pack more alternating regions of movement and compression into the tube.

teaching.text: Compression and movement play the roles of spring and mass.
children: Crowded air pushes back toward normal spacing, which supplies the restoring force.
Moving air keeps going because of inertia.
Together they keep the air oscillating around its usual positions.

teaching.text: Strong movement and strong compression occupy different places.
children: Where movement is large, the region carries a lot of moving mass.
Where spacing changes a lot, the region supplies strong restoring force while its central element stays nearly put.

teaching.text: Tracking one element over a cycle measures its movement, and tracking its gaps measures compression.
children: Added mass acts where movement is strong.
Added stiffness acts where compression is strong.

sections.title: The vocal-fold source sets harmonic spacing

teaching.text: The vocal folds produce the voiced **source**. Their repetition rate, **F0**, sets the spacing of the harmonic lines.
The top row recalls the **fixed–fixed membrane**, five modes and their sum.
children: A pickup point records the combined motion.
These frequencies were assigned for the illustration.

teaching.text: The bottom row shows **three source spectra** before filtering, each in the same **0 to 4000 Hz** window.
children: At **F0 = 100 Hz**, the harmonics crowd close together.
At **F0 = 250 Hz**, they sit at **250, 500, 750** and onward, from **tighter, lighter vocal folds**.
At **F0 = 350 Hz**, they sit at **350, 700, 1050** and onward, from **very tight and light vocal folds**.

teaching.text: **Lower F0 gives denser harmonic sampling, and higher F0 gives sparser sampling.**
children: Heavier, looser folds repeat more slowly.
Lighter, tighter folds repeat faster.
Mass slows the folds’ reversal, and tension speeds their return.

teaching.text: A voiced vowel holds **many frequencies** at once.
children: The source decides which harmonics are present.
The tract strengthens some regions and weakens others.
Pitch changes the source spacing, and vowel shape changes the tract’s favored regions.

sections.title: The vocal-tract filter favors nearby harmonics

teaching.text: The vocal tract is a **filter**, a **fixed–free** tube closed at one end and open at the other, and it selects **formants**.
children: A formant **encourages the closest harmonics to be audible**.
**Harmonics far from that formant are muted.**
The source supplies the harmonics, the filter decides which survive, and the vowel shape is the filter.

teaching.text: Each vowel sets its formants in its own places.
children: **Schwa** has well-separated first and second resonances, near **500** and **1500 Hz**.
**/u/** lowers both, near **300** and **1000 Hz**, and adds a third near **2000 Hz**.
**/i/ or /ɪ/** pairs a low F1 near **300 Hz** with a high F2 near **2200 Hz**.
**/a/** places its first two targets side by side at **800** and **900 Hz**.

teaching.text: Moving the tongue and lips moves these favored regions.
children: Each target lifts the harmonics closest to it.
Harmonics between targets stay weak.

teaching.text: A formant target belongs to the tract, and a harmonic line belongs to the source.
children: A target can sit between two lines and strengthen both neighbors.
Filtering adjusts the heights of the lines the source supplies.

sections.title: One filter can look different at different pitches

teaching.text: The grid crosses **source** rows with **vowel filter** columns to compare one filter at several pitches. **Dashed red ticks** mark formant targets, and **colored stems** mark the harmonics after filtering.
Each row holds one source.
children: The top row comes from **heavy, loose** folds with dense harmonics.
The middle row comes from **lighter, tighter** folds at **F0 = 250 Hz**.
The bottom row comes from the **lightest, tightest** folds at **F0 = 350 Hz**.

teaching.text: Each column holds one vowel filter.
children: Down a column, only F0 changes.
Across a row, only the filter changes.
The grid separates source effects from tract-shape effects.

teaching.text: **Dense harmonics trace the formant shape well.**
children: At low F0, many stems fall near each resonance.
Their heights draw the filter’s **envelope**, the smooth outline of favored strengths.
More harmonics in the window give a smoother, clearer spectrum.

teaching.text: **Sparse harmonics can miss a formant or make it look ambiguous.**
children: At high F0, the stems spread out.
A strong stem can sit beside a target, while the target stays where it was.
The two close /a/ targets can merge into one grouped region.

teaching.text: The resonances are all still present.
children: The ticks hold their positions down every column.
Unchanged ticks with wider stems mean the source changed while the filter stayed the same.

sections.title: Map spectra into a spectrogram

teaching.text: A **spectrum** captures **one instant**, while a **spectrogram** **stacks many spectra over time**.
children: In a spectrum, frequency runs across and peak height gives amplitude.
The sequence holds three slices of **/i/** and then three of **/a/**.

teaching.text: First, each spectrum’s frequency axis becomes the spectrogram’s **vertical axis**.
children: The slices line up from left to right in time.
Frequency now runs up the page.

teaching.text: Second, **height becomes darkness**.
children: **Black** is high amplitude, **gray** is medium and **white** is low.
A band that rises moves to a higher frequency.
A band that darkens gets stronger at its current frequency.

teaching.text: The horizontal axis means different things in the two displays.
children: In a spectrum, rightward means higher frequency.
In a spectrogram, rightward means later time.

teaching.text: From **/i/** to **/a/**, the first strong band **rises** and the second **falls**.
children: An upper band also moves down, and a fainter band stays high.
Linking neighboring slices traces the changing resonances, with position giving frequency and darkness giving strength.

sections.title: Reflection prompt
Speech-complexity experiment prompt
Use formants as input to vowel recognition

teaching.text: Speech science leads straight **back to AI**. A **neural network** will be trained on students’ **formants** and will decide which vowel is being spoken.
The inputs are **F1** and **F2**.
children: They are the first two resonance regions the vocal tract emphasizes.
Together they make a compact pair of numbers that characterizes each vowel.

teaching.text: The **input** and the **output** hold different information.
children: The input is a pair of sound measurements.
The output picks one vowel category.
The measured pair is evidence about the sound, and the true label names the category. Recognition connects one to the other.

teaching.text: The task ties the physics of speech to machine learning.
children: The mass–spring account explains where F1 and F2 come from.
The network learns how those numbers map onto vowel categories.
Training and testing will measure how well it does that.

sections.title: A fully connected linear vowel network

teaching.text: A **purely linear network** runs **2 inputs** through **hidden layers of 3, 2 and 4 neurons** to **5 outputs**, with **no activation functions**.
children: The inputs are **F1** and **F2**, kept in that order.

teaching.text: Every layer is **fully connected**.
children: Each receiving neuron links to every neuron in the layer before.
Every link has a **weight**.
A receiving neuron multiplies each incoming value by its weight and sums the results.

teaching.text: The hidden layers form intermediate combinations.
children: They hold **three**, then **two**, then **four** neurons.
Each hidden value is a weighted blend of what came before.
Different weights produce different blends of the same inputs.

teaching.text: The outputs name five words.
children: In order, they are **/done/, /dune/, /dean/, /Don/** and **/Dan/**.
The fixed order keeps each output tied to its word.

teaching.text: **Purely linear** means each layer hands its weighted sums straight to the next.
children: The whole computation is a chain of weighted sums.
A separate step would be needed to turn the five final values into probabilities.

sections.title: Random weights assign signed contributions to connections

teaching.text: One example input is **F1 = 320** and **F2 = 2000**, and **every edge gets a random weight**.
children: The inputs measure the sound.
The **weights** control how the network combines those measurements.
New weights give new internal results for the same input pair.

teaching.text: Each connection carries one weight.
children: A neuron multiplies incoming values by their weights and adds the products.
A first-layer neuron receives F1 and F2, so it has two incoming weights.
The three first-layer neurons build three different combinations of the same pair.

teaching.text: Before training, **every weight is a random number between −1 and 1**.
children: Edges carry values such as **0.95**, **−0.91** and **0.28**.
The heading marks **blue as positive** and **orange as negative**, and the negative edges render green in the figure. The written signs give direction and the sizes give strength.
Signed contributions can reinforce or oppose each other.

teaching.text: The weights are **random starting values**.
children: A **forward pass** runs an example through the current weights.
**Learning** adjusts those weights so the outputs come to match the vowel categories.

sections.title: Forward flow and an illustrative output distribution

teaching.text: In the **forward flow**, the input travels forward **layer by layer**, and the output is **a distribution over the five words**.
children: The animation moves the input pair along the connections, one layer at a time.
Each layer combines the previous layer’s values with its current weights.

teaching.text: The illustrated distribution gives each word a probability.
children: **/dune/**, **/dean/** and **/Don/** get **0.1** each.
/done/ is the favored prediction, and the rest keep some support.

teaching.text: A probability distribution has values between zero and one that add up to one, and these five do.
The bars picture the intended kind of output.
children: A purely linear network needs an extra step to guarantee a distribution.
The bars therefore stand for the goal of the forward pass.

teaching.text: The **predicted category** is the one the model favors.
children: The **true category** is the example’s actual label.
Comparing the two tells whether the prediction is correct.

sections.title: Declare the layer sequence in PyTorch

teaching.text: **PyTorch** expresses the same network in a few lines.
children: **import torch** loads the library.
**import torch.nn as nn** loads its neural-network tools as **nn**.
The model is stored in **net**.

teaching.text: **nn.Sequential** lists the layers in the order information flows through them.
children: A comment labels the shape purely linear, **2 to 3 to 2 to 4 to 5**.
Every **nn.Linear** layer computes weighted sums of its inputs.

teaching.text: The four layers mirror the picture.
children: **nn.Linear(2, 3, bias=False)** maps 2 inputs to 3 outputs.
**nn.Linear(3, 2, bias=False)** maps 3 to 2.
**nn.Linear(2, 4, bias=False)** maps 2 to 4.
**nn.Linear(4, 5, bias=False)** maps 4 to 5.
Each output count equals the next input count, so the values pass cleanly through, ending in five values for the five words.

teaching.text: **nn.Linear(in, out)** stores an **out × in weight matrix**, one weight for each connection.
children: **bias=False** drops the constant that a layer could add to each sum.
Every layer stays a **pure linear map**, as in the picture, with all of its weights in place.

teaching.text: The code is a **declaration only, with no training**.
children: It defines the structure.
Training would add examples and a procedure for adjusting the weights.

lecture15.title: Neural Networks · Forward propagation, learning, and sigmoid

sections.title: Neural Networks
Two formants feed a fully connected network

teaching.text: Two formants, **F1** and **F2**, go into the vowel network, and five responses come out, one each for **done, dune, dean, Don** and **Dan**.
children: The input positions hold measurements of the sound.
The output positions hold the network’s response to each word.

teaching.text: **Hidden layers** of **three, two and four** neurons sit in between.
children: The full layout is **2 to 3 to 2 to 4 to 5**, counting neurons per layer.
Each hidden neuron takes values from the layer before and passes its result to the layer after.

teaching.text: The layers are **fully connected**.
children: Each neuron feeds every neuron in the next layer.
Every connection has its own **weight**, and **40** signed weights fill the network, from small values like **+0.005** and **−0.001** to larger ones like **+0.6** and **−0.4**.
A positive weight passes its contribution on with the same sign, and a negative weight flips it.

teaching.text: F1 and F2 each reach all three first-layer neurons through different weights.
children: Every first-layer neuron therefore blends the same two measurements in its own proportions.

teaching.text: These weights hold steady across the network’s examples.
children: A new formant value changes what flows along the connections.
A new weight changes how strongly a connection counts.
Each weight describes one connection’s contribution to its receiving neuron.

sections.title: Forward propagation combines weighted inputs

teaching.text: **Forward propagation** moves information from the inputs through each hidden layer to the outputs, here for **F1 = 320** and **F2 = 2000**.
The top first-layer neuron computes **w₁ times F1 plus w₂ times F2**.
children: With weights **+0.005** and **−0.001**, F1 adds +0.005 times 320 and F2 adds −0.001 times 2000.
The total is **−0.40**.

teaching.text: That multiply-and-add operation is an **inner product**.
children: The other first-layer neurons, with their own weights, reach **6.64** and **2.72**.
Negative values like −0.40 pass forward just like positive ones.

teaching.text: Every later layer applies the same operation to the layer before it.
children: The second layer reaches about **5.50** and **−5.93**.
The third reaches about **1.57, −1.95, −1.95** and **−2.88**.
Each layer waits on the previous one, so information moves strictly in order.
**Softmax** raises e to each logit and divides by the total of all five exponentials.
The results are five positive probabilities that add to 1, even for negative logits.

teaching.text: **Done** comes out highest, at about **55.7%**.
children: **Don** follows at about 18.5%, then **Dan** at 10.2%, **dean** at **8.1%** and **dune** at 7.4%.
These are the current responses of a network with linear hidden activations and fixed weights.

sections.title: Pop quiz · Forward propagation
Info on Exam 2 and Exam 3
Backpropagation uses the difference between prediction and target

teaching.text: **Backpropagation** begins with two versions of the output.
children: The **computed output** is the network’s current distribution, with **done** at **55.7%** and **dean** at **8.1%**.
The **desired output** marks **dean** with a **1** and the other words with **0**, since dean is the word spoken.

teaching.text: **Cross-entropy loss** scores the mismatch from the probability of the true word.
children: Here the loss is the negative log of the probability of dean.
More probability on dean means less loss.

teaching.text: The computation moves **backward** from the outputs toward the inputs.
children: It finds the contribution of the final weights first.
It then works through hidden layer 3, hidden layer 2 and hidden layer 1, in that order.
Each step updates a layer’s weights, so **+0.1** becomes **+0.083** and **+0.6** becomes **+0.622**, for example.

teaching.text: A **gradient** gives how the loss shifts with a small change in one weight.
children: The update subtracts the learning rate, **η**, times that gradient from the weight.
A positive gradient lowers the weight, and a negative gradient raises it.

teaching.text: The forward-pass activations stay fixed during the whole backward pass.
children: Every gradient uses the original weights and stored activations, which makes the updates one simultaneous step.
A fresh forward pass then gives the updated predictions.
Input connections get a much smaller learning rate, since their inputs are raw formant values in hertz.

sections.title: Predict how changing a marked weight affects error

teaching.text: **If this weight increases, does the error go up or down?** The target word is **dean**, while the network favors **done**, so the answer depends on how the change moves the probability of dean.
The **pink** connection runs from the top neuron of the last hidden layer to **done**.
children: The weight is positive, and the neuron’s activation is about **1.57**.
Raising the weight raises done’s score.
Softmax splits one total among the five words, so a stronger done leaves less for dean, and the loss **rises**.

teaching.text: The **blue** connection runs from **F1** to the top neuron of the first hidden layer.
children: Raising it raises that neuron’s value, since F1 is positive.
The change then spreads through many signed connections to all five outputs.
Its effect on the error comes from all of those downstream paths together.

teaching.text: The backward calculation gives the answer for this network and target.
children: The blue connection’s gradient is positive as well.
A small increase raises the error, so the update lowers the weight.
Both marked weights decrease here, the early one because of the combined pull of every path that follows it.

sections.title: Backpropagation reuses downstream error calculations

teaching.text: Comparing the **last** weights with the **first** weights reveals why training runs backward.
The **last weights, W5**, set the output probabilities directly.
children: The error depends very directly on them.
The gap between computed and desired outputs points straight to better W5 values.

teaching.text: The **first weights, W2**, sit far from the error.
children: W2 shapes the first hidden activations.
Those pass through two more layers and other weights before any output appears.
W2’s share of the blame is spread across every path that follows it.
That share **includes** the effect of W5, since W5 lies downstream.

teaching.text: **W5 is the easy problem**, and W2 builds on it.
children: Solving small problems first and reusing their answers for larger, dependent problems is **dynamic programming**.
**Backpropagation is Bellman–Viterbi dynamic programming.**
It computes the output-side effects once and reuses them for each earlier layer.

teaching.text: **Backpropagation = SGD + dynamic programming.**
children: **SGD**, stochastic gradient descent, adjusts the weights.
Backpropagation supplies the gradients SGD needs, efficiently, through dynamic programming.

sections.title: Pair each recording with its target row

teaching.text: Training draws on two **training matrices**.
**Formant_Inputs** is **110 × 2**.
children: Each row holds **F1** and **F2** in hertz for one recording.
The network reads each row as one example.

teaching.text: **TrueVowel_Outputs** is **110 × 5**.
children: Its columns are **done, dune, dean, Don** and **Dan**.
Each row has a **1** in the correct word’s column and **0** elsewhere, a **one-hot** target.

teaching.text: Example rows pair formants with words.
children: **320, 2000** with **dean**, the network’s running example.

teaching.text: Row order ties the two matrices together.
children: The third input row, 320 and 2000, matches the third target row, dean.
Each input row stays with its own target row throughout training.
The five rows lay out the format of all 110 examples.

teaching.text: The network’s output and the target matrix are separate.
children: Before backpropagation, the network favors **done** at 55.7% for the dean example.
The target holds the correct label, and training compares the two.

sections.title: Read one full-batch training step in PyTorch

teaching.text: A short **PyTorch** program carries out one full-batch training step.
It first loads the data.
children: **X = torch.load("Formant_Inputs.pt").float()** brings in the 110 × 2 formants.
**Y = torch.load("TrueVowel_Outputs.pt").float()** brings in the 110 × 5 targets.
**.float()** gives both floating-point values, and the files are expected to exist already.

teaching.text: **nn.Sequential** declares the layers.
children: **nn.Linear(2, 3)**, **nn.Linear(3, 2)**, **nn.Linear(2, 4)** and **nn.Linear(4, 5)** follow the **2 to 3 to 2 to 4 to 5** layout.
The layers connect directly, with no declared activation in between.

teaching.text: Five lines make one training step.
children: **sgd = torch.optim.SGD(net.parameters(), lr=0.1)** prepares stochastic gradient descent at a **learning rate of 0.1**.
**sgd.zero_grad()** clears old gradients.
**loss = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()(net(X), Y)** runs the network and compares its scores with Y, with the softmax-related step built into the loss.
**loss.backward()** computes every parameter’s gradient.
**sgd.step()** updates the parameters.

teaching.text: Each line does one job.
children: Gradients are computed by backward and applied by step.
All **110 rows** feed this single step.
The program starts from PyTorch’s default weights and biases, so it shares the drawing’s layer sizes with its own starting numbers.

sections.title: Sigmoid turns an inner product into a bounded activation

teaching.text: The **sigmoid activation function**, **σ(z) = 1 / (1 + exp(−z))**, turns an inner product z into a value between 0 and 1.
Large inputs land near the limits.
children: A **large positive** inner product gives a sigmoid near **1**.
A **large negative** inner product gives a sigmoid near **0**.

teaching.text: The curve is an S.
children: The **linear activation**, the weighted sum, runs along the horizontal axis, and the **sigmoid activation** runs up the vertical axis.
It climbs steeply through the middle and levels off at both ends.
On the flat ends, large input changes produce only small output changes.

teaching.text: In the formula, a large positive z shrinks exp(−z) toward zero, pushing the output toward 1.
children: A large negative z makes exp(−z) enormous, pushing the output toward 0.

teaching.text: **Lord Edgar Adrian**, **Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, 1932**, provides the biological motivation.
children: **Neurons are nearly digital**, roughly on or off.
His work concerned firing rates, and the sigmoid models that graded, nearly on-off behavior.

teaching.text: **Animal perception** follows the same pattern.
children: Some similar things are perceived as different, and some very different things are perceived as the same.
Inputs on either side of the steep middle give very different outputs, while inputs on a flat end give nearly identical ones.

sections.title: Apply sigmoid while recalculating downstream activity

teaching.text: Sigmoid is added to the network **one neuron at a time**, with the inputs held at **F1 = 320** and **F2 = 2000** and every weight unchanged.
children: **Purple** marks a linear neuron.
**Green** marks a neuron that passes its inner product through sigmoid.
The nine hidden neurons switch in layer order, three, then two, then four.

teaching.text: The first switch takes the top first-layer neuron from **−0.400** to about **0.401**.
children: The next layer now receives a different value.
Every downstream value is **recalculated** from that point forward.
The result is a true sigmoid network, built one neuron at a time.

teaching.text: With the first layer all sigmoid, its outputs are about **0.401, 0.999** and **0.938**.
children: The second layer then gives about **0.713** and **0.223**.
The third layer ends at about **0.599, 0.609, 0.609** and **0.481**.

teaching.text: The outputs still go through **softmax**.
children: Once every hidden neuron uses sigmoid, **Dan** leads at about **32.0%**.
**Dean** climbs to about **23.0%**, **dune** sits near 20.2%, **done** drops to about 16.2% and **Don** is near 8.5%.
Same inputs, same weights, different output pattern.

teaching.text: The weights have not been trained.
children: Dean improves over the all-linear network and still trails Dan.
Changing the activation rule changes the network’s favorite, and training is what aligns that favorite with the true word.

sections.title: Insert sigmoid after the hidden linear layers

teaching.text: This PyTorch program repeats the earlier one with **sigmoid** added after each hidden layer.
children: It loads **X**, the 110 × 2 formants, and **Y**, the 110 × 5 targets, exactly as before.
**nn.Sigmoid()** follows **nn.Linear(2, 3)**, **nn.Linear(3, 2)** and **nn.Linear(2, 4)**.

teaching.text: The sizes stay **2 to 3 to 2 to 4 to 5**.
children: Sigmoid reshapes values while keeping their count.
Three values remain three, so **nn.Linear(3, 2)** still gets the input size it expects.
The two-value and four-value layers work the same way.

teaching.text: **nn.Linear(4, 5)** ends the network with no sigmoid after it.
children: Its five logits go to **CrossEntropyLoss**, which carries out the softmax-related calculation.
Hidden sigmoids transform intermediate values, while the final layer scores the five words.

teaching.text: The training lines stay the same.
children: **zero_grad**, the forward pass with its loss, **backward** and **step** run in that order.
The learning rate stays **0.1**, and all 110 recordings feed one step.

teaching.text: The drawn network uses the original illustrative weights with no biases, giving Dan **32.0%** and dean **23.0%**.
children: The program begins with PyTorch’s default weights and biases.
Its structure matches the drawing, and the same starting weights and bias choices would reproduce the drawing’s probabilities.
